blocks.text: On the dove's feathers, neck, eyes, moaning and flight.

I am pleased to begin the description of the dove with its plumage and feathers, whose beauty [col. 9] the sacred poet commends thus, Psal. LXVIII, 14.: The wings of the dove covered with silver, and its feathers with the paleness of gold. Wings and feathers stand here by συνεκδοχὴν [synekdochēn] for the whole body. Covered with silver, that is, supremely white like silver, and bright with a certain splendour. For silver is called in Greek ἀργύριον [argyrion], from τὸ ἀργὸν, τὸ λευκόν [to argon, to leukon, "the bright, the white"]; and things that are most brilliantly white are called silver. Hence in the poets ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις [argyropeza Thetis], that is, λευκόπους [leukopous]. So it is in Hesychius, who likewise explains ἀργυροδίνην κρήνην [argyrodinēn krēnēn] as λευκὰ ῥεύματα ἔχουσαν [leuka rheumata echousan]; and in the eighth book of the Aeneid,
is, on the testimony of Servius, an epithet of colour. The raven too was once a silver bird, when it equalled doves in whiteness. Ovid, Metam. book 2, Fable 7:

For this was once a silver bird with snowy feathers, so that it equalled doves wholly without blemish. [II, 534] For among doves some are extremely white ^{(1)}. Varro, On Agriculture book 3, ch. 7: The other kind of doves is the tamer, which, content with household food, is usually fed within the threshold of the door. This kind is mostly white in colour. That is, at some times and in some places, not always nor everywhere. For in Greece white doves were seen late, namely when the forces of Xerxes were routed at Mount Athos. This is expressly reported in the Persica by Charon of Lampsacus, who lived at that time and wrote before Herodotus. Athenaeus, book 9: Χάρων δ᾽ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς, ἐν τοῖς Περσικοῖς περὶ Μαρδονίου ἱστορῶν, καὶ τοῦ διαφθαρέντος στρατοῦ Περσικοῦ περὶ τὸν Ἄθω, γράφει ταῦτα· „Καὶ λευκαὶ περιστεραὶ τότε πρῶτον εἰς „Ἕλληνας ἐφάνησαν, πρότερον οὐ γιγνόμεναι“ [Charōn d᾽ ho Lampsakēnos, en tois Persikois peri Mardoniou historōn, kai tou diaphtharentos stratou Persikou peri ton Athō, graphei tauta: "Kai leukai peristerai tote prōton eis Hellēnas ephanēsan, proteron ou gignomenai"]. Charon of Lampsacus, in the Persica, treating of Mardonius and of the Persian army routed at Mount Athos, writes this: "And white doves were then first seen among the Greeks, there having been none before", namely in Greece, not anywhere, as the translator there wrongly has it. Aelian in the Varia book 1, ch. 15: Χάρων δὲ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς περὶ τὸν Ἄθω φανῆναι περιστερὰς λευκὰς λέγει, ὅτε ἐνταῦθα ἀπώλοντο αἱ τῶν Περσῶν τριέρεις παρακάμπτουσαι τὸν Ἄθω [Charōn de ho Lampsakēnos peri ton Athō phanēnai peristeras leukas legei, hote entautha apōlonto hai tōn Persōn triereis parakamptousai ton Athō]; But Charon of Lampsacus asserts that white doves were seen around Athos when the triremes of the Persians perished there while sailing past Athos. There follows in the Psalm ואברותיה בירקרק חרוץ, And its feathers with the paleness of gold; supply covered, which must be repeated from the preceding hemistich. Paleness of gold, that is, gold of paleness, or pale gold. Similar is Habac. II, 6. עב טיט, thickness of mud, for mud of thickness, or thick mud. התואר במקום המתואר, the predicate for the subject, as Kimchi has it here. Gold is called חרוץ charuts, that is, dug out of the earth, here and in Zach. IX, 3. and frequently in Solomon's Proverbs ^{(2)}. From this comes the Greek χρυσός [chrysos]. And the paleness of gold is ירקרק, with doubled letters, so that the meaning is intensified. Accordingly from this very word comes the Ethiopic ወርቅ፡ vvark for gold. The Greek translators rightly call the paleness of gold χλωρότητα χρυσίου [chlōrotēta chrysiou]. For this is the true colour of gold. Hence Diogenes, asked Διὰ τί τὸ χρυσίον χλωρόν ἐστιν; [Dia ti to chrysion chlōron estin?] Why [II, 535] is gold pale?, answered Ὅτι πολλοὺς ἔχει τοὺς ἐπιβουλεύοντας [Hoti pollous echei tous epibouleuontas], Because it has many plotting against it. So it is in Laertius; and Catullus in the wedding of Peleus and Thetis,
O how often she grew paler than the sallow hue of gold!
A guest paler than a gilded statue.
And Statius to Maximus Junius in the fourth book of the Silvae,
When will the Dalmatian mountains send you back to sweet Latium, where, having seen Dis, the pale miner returns, of the same colour as the gold he has dug up?
